Autonomous closed-loop discovery of organic laser materials

Abstract
We present a self-driving laboratory that combines robotic synthesis with Bayesian optimization to autonomously discover organic laser materials. The platform performs closed-loop experimentation across thousands of candidate molecules and identifies six new gain media within three weeks of operation.

Introduction
The discovery of high-performance organic laser molecules has traditionally relied on intuition-driven synthesis followed by manual characterization. Closed-loop autonomous laboratories promise to compress this iteration cycle by integrating active learning, robotic chemistry, and on-line characterization.

Methods
Our autonomous platform comprises a six-axis robotic arm, an on-line UV/Vis-fluorescence module, and a workflow orchestration layer based on the open-source ChemOS package. We integrate Bayesian optimization over a 12-dimensional reaction-condition space; the surrogate model is a Gaussian process with an anisotropic Matern-5/2 kernel. Each closed-loop experimentation cycle synthesizes one candidate, measures gain via amplified spontaneous emission, and updates the posterior.

Results
The closed-loop campaign converged within 482 experiments. We report six molecules with gain coefficients exceeding 80 cm^-1. A control experiment using random sampling required >3000 experiments to recover equivalent performance.

Figure 1. Autonomous closed-loop platform for materials discovery. The schematic shows the integration of robotic synthesis, automated characterization, and Bayesian optimization in a self-driving laboratory configuration.

Figure 2. Discovered organic laser molecules ranked by gain coefficient.

Discussion
This work demonstrates that closed-loop optimization combined with high-throughput experimentation can accelerate organic materials discovery by an order of magnitude over conventional approaches.
